newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ interest rates won't fall far - BNZ Sept review.
newsitem.headline: NZ interest rates won't fall far - BNZ Sept review.

text.p: New Zealand interest rates would not fall far during the downward leg of their cycle, the Bank of New Zealand said in its September Economic Review released on Tuesday.
Rates would fail to fall far because of short and medium term upward risks to inflation, the bank said in the quarterly review.
"We believe there are medium term upward risks facing inflation stemming from our forecast of a strong lift in the economic cycle from early 1997," it said.
Signs of an economic upturn were imminent, BNZ said, citing rising demand for credit within the bank.

Its concern about inflation reflected several factors: low availability of spare labour, little spare office space, an over-valued exchange rate, the likelihood of easier fiscal policy, and an expected further rise in house prices.
"It is extremely unlikely the NZ dollar will continue its recent rise and we forecast four percent depreciation from March 1997 to March 1998," the bank said.

Looser fiscal policy was expected whatever the make-up of the next government after Saturday's inconclusive election. The Reserve Bank had explicitly warned this could mean firmer monetary conditions were required to achieve the same inflation profile.
BNZ also said business and consumer confidence had rebounded strongly from lows in May/June.

"It is likely that interest rates will not only fail to fall far during the downward leg of their cycle, but will be rising far earlier than the near three years it took from the start of the 1991 upturn. We think rates will be rising within 12 months
of the next economic upturn starting," it said.
"Our outlook implies potentially very tight monetary policy from late-1997 which should cause a sharp contraction in household spending during 1998."
